# SLIDE WRITING GUIDELINES {.section-divider}

*Delete this whole section when you copy the template. It is the agreed standard for every lecture, derived from review of L1–L3.*

## Audience and Level

- The audience is mostly **nursing students**, plus PSEO (high-schoolers), gen-ed, and some pre-meds. Write for a **capable 12th grader**.
- Anything a 12th grader wouldn't know (an RCT, germline vs. somatic, brain death, a legal standard) gets a tight plain-language explanation the first time — usually in a `.context-box`.
- **Show, don't just name.** Don't write "Willowbrook exposed institutional failure"; tell what concretely happened to real, named people. Conclusions land only after the story.
- Distressing history (Nazi experiments, Tuskegee, sterilization): **concrete but restrained** — name what was done plainly, no graphic detail.

## Slide Density (hard rule)

Every Reveal.js slide must fit **one 1050×700 screen** with no scrolling. Prefer splitting or grid-based structuring over cramming.
- **Single-Column Lists:** Limit to 3-4 bullets maximum if they are full sentences. Never use 6 detailed single-column bullets, as they will cause a vertical overflow on standard viewports.
- **Content Budget:** A content slide carries **50 to 70 words, and never more than about 90**. That is deliberately more than a standard slide, so that students do not have to take heavy notes, but nobody should have to read a paragraph off the screen. Use full sentences, at most two in a row, and usually three one-sentence bullets.
- **What stays on the slide:** what a student would otherwise write down: names, dates, numbers, definitions, and the one-sentence claim. Cut the second example, the aside, and the connective prose.
- **Where the rest goes:** asynchronous students get a video plus the HTML notes, so transitions and extra detail belong in an HTML-only block: `::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}`. Do not write the same passage twice, once for each format.
- **Deck Budget:** each lecture part has **20 to 30 content slides** (fewer when they are dense) and **3 to 4 question slides**.
- **Multi-Column Splits:** Use two-column grids (`::: {.columns}`) to split longer lists, compare concepts, or place a `.callout` next to text. This doubles the usable screen width and keeps heights low.

## Study-Worthiness

- Each content slide must teach on its own: real **names, dates, numbers, mechanisms, and outcomes**, not gestures.
- Cut navigational filler ("the next slides will trace…", "as mentioned earlier"). It wastes the word budget; a transition belongs in an HTML-only block.
- If a slide is only a slogan, it is not done.

## Layout Variety & Slide Design

Monotony is a defect. **Never run more than two plain bullet-list slides in a row.** Leverage reveal.js columns and custom layouts to create a premium, designed look:

- **Two-Column comparative layout:** Use side-by-side columns (`::: {.columns}`) of equal width (e.g. `width="48%"` with a central spacer `width="4%"`). Perfect for comparing "The Distinction vs. The Application" or two opposing views.
- **Card and Callout Integrations:** Place a case study or a crucial definition inside a `.callout-note` or `.callout-important` box in one column, while keeping key analytical points as clean bullets in the opposite column. This prevents slides from feeling "sparse" while keeping vertical height tight.
- **2x2 Grid Layouts:** For list structures like definitions or candidate criteria, use two columns with short bold headers. This creates a clean quadrant grid that is highly legible.
- **Tables and Cards:** Use comparative tables or `.quote-card` blocks to collapse parallel details into single, high-contrast slides.

| Shape | Use for |
|---|---|
| Two-column **split grid** | Splitting long lists, comparisons, concept grids, and card combinations |
| Two-column **text + image** | Any slide with a photo — the image is a *column*, never dumped under bullets |
| Contrast / comparison table | Competing standards or collapsed parallel concepts (e.g., Belmont principles) |
| Quote-card | Primary-source quotation (see Quotes) |
| `.context-box` | A mini-case or a concept a 12th grader needs |
| Timeline / flow `{dot}` | Sequences and decision procedures |
| Summary "scoreboard" table | Truly parallel cases, gathered once (see Recurring Devices) |

Collapse repetitive parallel runs (three near-identical principle slides → one rich table or one beautiful comparison grid). Consolidating and *then* enriching beats leaving thin, parallel slides.

## Discussion Units

Each lecture part has **3 to 4 question slides**, about 10 minutes each. More than that crowds out the content. A unit is built from these pieces; only the first is required:

1. **`## Thought Question`** — a concrete scenario with **one or two questions** (put the student in a role). Keep the scenario **under about 50 words**: the slide stays up for the whole discussion, and the questions are what students need to see.
2. **`## Make It Contemporary`** (optional) — a **documented present-day analogue** (real law, case, study, or practice). It counts as a question slide.
3. **`## After You've Discussed`** (optional) — a `.callout-note` debrief that introduces a **new distinction the body never stated** (e.g., coercion vs. undue inducement vs. exploitation). It must *advance* the analysis, never merely restate the lecture. It counts as a content slide.

A question can do one of three jobs. Mix them; do not use one job for every unit.

- **Hook**, before the content. Students commit to an answer, and the section that follows responds to it. A hook needs no debrief slide. The opening case is always a hook.
- **Transition**, between two sections.
- **Application or review**, after the content.

**No delivery directions on the slide.** The same deck is taught face to face and asynchronously, so never write "discuss with a neighbour" or "show of hands". Word a commitment so that it works for someone reading alone: "Pick one before you read on."

### Writing questions that start a discussion

The test for every question: **could two thoughtful students give opposite answers and both be defensible?** If not, it is a comprehension check, and it belongs in the Review Questions.

- **Ask for experience.** Each unit needs at least one question students can answer from their own lives, before any course vocabulary: "Has an algorithm ever made a call about you that you couldn't see inside?" Offer several ways in (work, family, school, the unit) so nobody has to disclose something private to take part.
- **Ask for a commitment.** Make them vote, rank, pick a number, or set a threshold, then ask what would change their mind. Come back to an opening vote at the end of the lecture.
- **Grant the other side its best point.** If the patient, parent, or skeptic in the scenario is partly right, say so in the stem. Then ask what follows.
- **Ask what they would say or do, in the room.** Practice questions ("What do you say to her in the next sixty seconds?") have many good answers. Analysis questions usually have one.
- **Do not hide an answer in the question.** Avoid "What's the flaw in…", "Name the mistake precisely", "Does that settle it?", "Is X really the same as Y?", and "Which thinker would say…". All of them tell students you are holding the answer.
- **Do not ask them to recall the lecture.** "Which of the 3 Rs applies?" is a review question.
- **The debrief is a lens, not the answer key.** Open it with "one way to see this" or "however you voted", never with what the scenario "turns on". Say what the distinction leaves unsettled. If students learn that the next slide reveals the answer, they will wait for it.

## Quotes

- A stand-alone quote slide uses a **longer, verbatim** passage, not a clipped phrase.
- **Verbatim accuracy is non-negotiable.** Verify against a primary or authoritative source; reproduce punctuation exactly; mark editorial changes with `[brackets]` and cuts with an ellipsis.
- Attribute fully, including **translator/edition** for translated works (e.g., Kant, Abbott trans.).

## Cross-References and Metacommentary

- **Never use `L#` codes** ("L7", "see L2") — students don't know them and numbering changes.
- **No inter-lecture metacommentary** in slides ("as we saw in Lecture 2", "Part B will not re-tell this"). Use plain phrasing: *"later, when we turn to end-of-life care."*
- Treat earlier lectures as **prior knowledge**: recap in one line, then apply — don't re-teach. Minimize overlap between lectures by design.

## Citations

- Use real `refs.bib` keys only. **Never invent a key.** If a source should be cited, add a correct entry to `refs.bib` first.
- Contemporary facts (recent laws, cases, figures) may be stated in prose **without** a citation, consistently — but get them factually right.

## Banned Patterns

- "Read for next class" / reading-assignment slides.
- Slides whose whole body is 3–4 terse fragments.
- Long parallel runs of "X is not Y" / one-word bullets.
- Re-narrating a case already told in full in an earlier lecture.

## Recurring Devices (encouraged)

- Every lecture part has a **spine**: one central question, stated on the "Today" slide and answered in the recap. A single patient followed across the lecture can carry it.
- **Do not overuse a table motif.** A summary scoreboard that gathers truly parallel cases is worth one slide, near the end. Repeating the same table shape for each case in turn is monotony; say it in a sentence instead.

## Dialogue Slides (occasional)

A short cartoon conversation can stage a case: patient and clinician, or two clinicians. Use the cast in `images/characters/figures/` (see `images/characters/cast.md` and `cast.png`). Keep it to three or four short exchanges, and use it to *pose* the problem, not to model the answer the discussion should reach.

# Part A — [Subtitle] {.section-divider}

## Opening: A Case to Sit With

Open with a concrete scenario that frames the lecture's central tension — usually a `.thought-question` (the hook, not the lesson), followed by a short `.callout-note` "After You've Discussed". Make students feel the problem before they get vocabulary.

## What We're Doing Today

::: {.learning-outcomes}
By the end of Part A, you will be able to:

- [Outcome: action verb + specific content; tell what *happened* in named cases, not just "discuss themes"]
- [Outcome]
- [Outcome]
:::

## [Section Title]

Body in **full sentences**. Introduce a [key term]{.key-term} the first time it appears. Keep to the density rule above.

In-text citations use Pandoc/Chicago author-date: @beauchamp2019 argued X; a parenthetical looks like this [@emanuel1992]; multiple at once [@beauchamp2019; @faden1986].

::: {.context-box}
**[Concept a 12th grader may not know]**

Two or three tight sentences of plain-language background. Scaffolding only.
:::

## [Section Title] — varied layout

Rotate the shape (table / two-column+image / quote-card / `dot`). For a diagram, prefer Graphviz `{dot}` or Mermaid (editable) over a static picture:

```{dot}
digraph G {
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style=rounded];
  "Refuses treatment" -> "Has capacity?";
  "Has capacity?" -> "Honor refusal" [label="yes"];
  "Has capacity?" -> "Surrogate decides" [label="no"];
}
```

## Thought Question

::: {.thought-question}
A concrete scenario (under about 50 words) in which the student has a role, with one or two questions: one that asks for their own experience, and one that asks them to commit to a position two students could defensibly split on.
:::

## Make It Contemporary

::: {.thought-question}
A documented present-day analogue (real law/case/study) that re-poses the same tension.
:::

## After You've Discussed

::: {.callout-note}
A debrief that introduces a **new distinction** — never a restatement of the slides above, and never the "right answer" to the question. Offer it as a lens, and say what it leaves open.
:::

## Mini-Recap

::: {.recap}
Two or three sentences synthesizing Part A and bridging into Part B.
:::

# Part B — [Subtitle] {.section-divider}

## Where We Left Off

One short paragraph reorienting a student who watched Part A separately. Online students see A then B back-to-back, so don't over-repeat.

## What We're Doing in Part B

::: {.learning-outcomes}
By the end of Part B, you will be able to:

- [Outcome]
- [Outcome]
:::

## [Section Title]

Build on Part A as prior knowledge (recap in a line, then apply). Same density and layout-variety rules. Run at least one full discussion unit.

## [Application Section]

Work a brief illustrative case in the text, or point to the paired case study **by its descriptive title, not a case number** (case titles carry no numbers):

> **Paired case:** [Descriptive Case Title](../cases/NN-slug.qmd)

## Wrap-Up

::: {.recap}
Three or four sentences summarizing the whole arc — the question, the main moves, the unresolved tension. No `L#`.
:::

## Review Questions

Write a brief answer to each, or use them as discussion prompts.

::: {.review-questions}

::: {.review-item .review-recall}
[Recall]{.review-label}

[Question text: retrieve definitions, distinctions, mechanisms, or framework maps from that lesson-part only]
:::

::: {.review-item .review-apply}
[Apply]{.review-label}

[Question text: use a new scenario, not the lesson's opening hook, running patient, paired case study, or existing Thought Question stem]
:::

::: {.review-item .review-debate}
[Debate]{.review-label}

[Question text: reserve one current controversy lane per lesson-part so later lessons do not reuse the same topic]
:::
